source.title: Claims: Abhinavagupta makes original philosophical arguments (yukti)
source.author: Codex/Hermes loop

claims.claim_text: In TĀ 4.8-9, Abhinavagupta presents an original pūrvapakṣa-siddhānta argument: the objection that self-awareness would make consciousness an object (and thus insentient) fails because consciousness is by its very nature (svabhāvāt) self-aware (svātmasaṃvitti). Self-awareness is not objectification — it is non-objectifying self-presence. This is presented as Abhinava's own reasoning (yukti), not a scripture quotation.
claims.hetu: the objection that self-awareness would objectify consciousness fails because self-awareness is not objectification
claims.sadhya: svasaṃvedana is the intrinsic nature of consciousness, not a second-order reflection
claims.vyapti_statement: If consciousness is by nature self-aware, then self-awareness is not a problem but the very condition for sentience.

falsifier.condition: Show that Abhinavagupta's argument in TĀ 4.8-9 depends on scriptural authority rather than reason, or that the objection he refutes is a straw man not held by any actual Buddhist opponent.

claims.claim_text: In TĀ 4.181cd-182ab, Abhinavagupta argues in his own voice that consciousness IS reflective awareness (parāmarśa) by nature, and its spontaneous resonance (dhvani) is the supreme Heart (mahā hṛdaya). This is one of his most fundamental philosophical claims: the nature of consciousness is self-awareness, and this self-awareness has a spontaneous, creative dimension (the seed mantra SAUḤ). The argument is presented as a conclusion from reasoning, not an appeal to scripture.
claims.hetu: consciousness is self-aware by nature, and this self-awareness is spontaneously creative
claims.sadhya: self-awareness is not static but dynamic — it is the creative Heart of reality
claims.vyapti_statement: If self-awareness is the nature of consciousness and is spontaneously creative, then svasaṃvedana is not merely cognitive but generative.

falsifier.condition: Show that the mahā hṛdaya argument depends on a specific scriptural tradition that Abhinavagupta is merely transmitting, not extending.
